name: ProgramBench
intro: ProgramBench 评估智能体仅凭只可执行标准程序与清理后文档，从零重建完整软件的能力。论文 v1 报告 200 个任务和 248,853 个隐藏行为测试；固定 v1.2.4 Git 树含 201 个任务目录（含包内测试夹具），活跃分支列出 313,292 个测试名，其中 65,845 个被忽略、247,447 个有效计分，因此页面明确区分论文与后续发布口径。
org: Meta FAIR, Meta TBD, Stanford University, Harvard University
build_method: Claude Sonnet 4.5 与 mini-SWE-agent 辅助的开源仓库转换、覆盖率驱动行为测试、弱断言与标准/虚假程序过滤、文档清理及只执行程序洁净镜像
eval_feature: 无网络黑盒重建；禁止源码查找、程序封装、反编译与跟踪；公开 CLI 解析隐藏 Pytest 的 JUnit 结果并过滤忽略项，论文另用九模型多数票作弊门；每题最多 1,000 步和 6 小时
scale: 论文v1：200个任务、248,853个测试函数、中位数770；固定Git v1.2.4：201个任务目录、活跃分支列出313,292个测试名，其中65,845个忽略、247,447个有效计分；固定HF：200个任务目录
build_method_en: Claude Sonnet 4.5 and mini-SWE-agent conversion of open-source repositories, coverage-guided behavioral tests, assertion plus gold/dummy filtering, documentation sanitization, and execute-only clean-room images
eval_feature_en: Offline black-box rebuilding with no source lookup, wrapping, decompilation, or tracing; the public CLI parses hidden Pytest JUnit results and ignored-test metadata, while the paper adds a separate nine-judge cheating gate; 1,000 steps and 6 hours per task
intro_en: ProgramBench evaluates whether agents can rebuild complete software from an execute-only reference program and sanitized documentation. Paper v1 reports 200 tasks and 248,853 hidden behavioral tests; the pinned v1.2.4 Git tree has 201 task directories, including a package test fixture, and 313,292 test names listed on active branches, of which 65,845 are ignored and 247,447 are effective for scoring, so the page separates paper and later-release counts.
scale_en: Paper v1: 200 tasks, 248,853 test functions, median 770; pinned Git v1.2.4: 201 task directories and 313,292 listed test names on active branches, with 65,845 ignored and 247,447 effective for scoring; pinned HF: 200 task directories

Therefore has_leaderboard is true; the earlier false value was not compatible with the official release. TASK FORMULATION: the task worker receives a gold executable, usage documentation, and essential assets, but not source code or hidden tests. It may choose any programming language and must write a complete source repository plus a compile script whose candidate executable reproduces the gold program's observable behavior. Internet is disabled. Evaluation tests may check standard output, standard error, exit codes, files, and other file-system side effects, but not source-level structure. Tests finite-sample the gold executable and therefore provide a lower bound on full behavioral equivalence. FOUR-STAGE CONSTRUCTION: paper Section 2.2 uses mini-SWE-agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5 in an Ubuntu 22.04 Docker container. Candidate repositories must be open source and produce a standalone executable or program; compiled-language repositories are a strong sourcing heuristic, not a rule that constrains the candidate's implementation language. First, the collection agent compiles the gold executable and records a single script reproducing the successful build. Second, it explores the executable, source, existing tests, and documentation, invokes the program with varied inputs, and writes behavioral tests in a Pytest harness. It harvests existing behavioral or integration tests when available. Third, it iteratively measures first-party line coverage, targets uncovered paths, and generates additional tests. Fourth, it removes source code, original tests, implementation details, local build artifacts, and dependency caches from the candidate-facing environment, sanitizes usage-related documentation, and injects the already compiled gold executable into an independent image. The gold executable is execute-only; essential assets that a model could not reasonably synthesize are included. TEST GENERATION AND FILTERING: Appendix A.3 compares monolithic, six-prompt decomposed, and coverage-guided iterative strategies. The paper adopts the coverage-guided loop: it harvests eligible existing tests, writes new tests, measures current coverage, and asks the agent to exercise missing paths. Reported analysis says 79.5% of tests are self-generated and 20.5% harvested. The assertion linter flags structurally weak cases including no assertions, trivially true assertions, exit-code-only checks, disjunctive assertions, short substrings, swallowed exceptions, weak length checks, and file-exists-only tests. Flagged tests are returned to the generation agent for repair. At the end, tests that do not pass the gold binary deterministically or that pass a dummy binary are discarded. The loop's static linter plus gold/dummy feedback reduces trivial dummy passes; the graph represents this as a repair loop, not a one-shot filter. PAPER DATASET: paper v1 states 200 task instances and 248,853 test functions, with a median of 770 tests per task. The 200 repositories span Rust, Go, C, C++, Java, and Haskell and range from small CLI utilities to FFmpeg, SQLite, DuckDB, PHP, Lua, tinycc, ripgrep, fzf, and jq. The benchmark does not require a native test suite: the paper finds 141 of 200 source repositories had tests and 59 did not. An audit of all 200 paper tasks found no tests invoking flags or subcommands absent from exposed documentation. The test suite remains an under-approximation; passing does not prove full semantic equivalence. CLEAN-ROOM ACCESS: the inference image exposes the execute-only gold program, sanitized documentation and permitted assets. The Appendix A.2 prompt forbids cloning, browsing, installing, or otherwise obtaining the project's source; forbids wrappers, shims, copies, pre-built substitutes, and runtime delegation to the original tool; and forbids decompilers, disassemblers, strace, ltrace, or similar binary-analysis tools. It permits ordinary interaction with the executable through flags, arguments, stdin/stdout, and bundled documentation. No-internet is enforced at container level. The paper baseline uses mini-SWE-agent with 20 CPUs, 60 GB RAM, at most 1,000 steps, and a six-hour wall-clock limit per task. All models use vendor-default hyperparameters. The task worker submits all created source code and a root compile.sh in submission.tar.gz. PUBLIC EVALUATION PIPELINE: v1.2.4's evaluator unpacks the submission into a clean workspace, removes files whose hash matches the original executable, blocks internet during compilation, makes compile.sh executable, and runs it. A build failure becomes an evaluation error rather than silently receiving a score. The evaluator loads tests.json metadata, selects non-ignored test branches, downloads per-branch archives on demand from the fixed HF dataset, and runs each hidden Pytest branch. It writes JUnit XML. parse_test_results maps testcases to passed, failure, error, skipped, system_error, or not_run; an expected test absent from XML becomes not_run, and conflicting duplicate result kinds become system_error. Unexpected tests are warned rather than added silently to the expected denominator. Per-test ignored entries from tests.json are removed before the score is computed. System and branch errors are preserved explicitly. The public docs recommend using programbench info rather than hand-counting raw JSON. METRICS: EvaluationResult.score is the fraction of expected, non-ignored test results whose status is passed. n_resolved counts passed test cases, while benchmark-level % Tests Passed captures per-instance partial progress. A paper-level instance is Resolved only when all associated tests pass and the run is not flagged as cheating. % Almost is the fraction of instances with at least 95% tests passed. The primary headline % Resolved is aggregated over the paper's 200 tasks; partial test pass rate is meaningful for relative comparisons but a single failed test can still represent a fundamental missing behavior.
